speechtext:
In introducing the foreign investment review bill for second reading, I wish to remind hon. members that this bill is only one of the measures on foreign investment which this government proposed in the Speech from the Throne. This bill is a major extension of the review process to cover, not only takeovers, but the establishment of new foreign-controlled businesses in Canada.
My department is preparing a bill as well, which I hope to introduce very shortly, to provide for the registration of technology transfer agreements. There will also be legislation providing that a majority of the board of directors of federally incorporated companies be Canadian. Measures to increase Canadian participation in the ownership and control of resource projects are under consideration. Lastly, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has proposed that the next meeting of first ministers examine the desirability of restricting sales of land to foreigners. It is against that kind of background that I want to speak this afternoon in introducing what I consider to be one of the most important bills, not only in this parliament, but in other parliaments from the point of view of the development of a distinctive Canada.
The government's purpose in introducing this bill is very simple. It is part of a package of measures designed to build that kind of Canada I have described, a vital and distinctive Canada. We already have in place a number of policies to support Canadian entrepreneurship and initiative. Others are under consideration. But we also need measures to ensure that initiatives inspired by non-Canadians are of significant benefit to Canada. Bill C-132 asks parliament for this power.
Foreign ownership policy is not an end in itself. Together with other measures, this bill will help to generate meaningful and satisfying employment for Canadians and promote economic growth. Moreover, there is a cultural and social as well an economic dimension to this measure. It can be seen I believe as a positive measure to help shape a positive Canadian identity. In this sense, the bill should be unique and distinctive, reflecting the reality of Canada. Canadian identity will be determined to the extent that Canadians acquire or increase their power to decide what their economy shall produce, what markets shall be served, what research and development will be undertaken. We want an economy which gives us power to innovate in response to a changing environment. If we lose this power, we turn control of our future over to those who retain it. In short, we have four objectives: one, to support the development of strong, Canadian-held business enterprises; two, to ensure that future foreign take-
Foreign Investment Review
overs and the establishment of new foreign-held businesses will be of significant benefit to Canada; three, to help arrest and reverse the increasing degree of foreign control of our economy; four, to contribute to the development of a distinctive Canadian identity.
Surely, no one in this House will dispute the propriety of these objectives at a time when foreign control of our economy is so extensive. Nearly 60 per cent of manufacturing industry in Canada is foreign-controlled, and in some manufacturing industries such as petroleum and rubber products foreign control exceeds 90 per cent. Recent figures for Canadian mining and smelting indicate that 65 per cent is controlled from abroad. Approximately 80 per cent of that foreign control over Canadian manufacturing and natural resources rests in the United States.
In offering these figures, I want in no way to downgrade the important role which foreign capital has played in the economic development of Canada. Foreign direct investment has brought us new products, new technology, managerial skills, access to foreign markets and the economies of scale which this implies, as well as improved productivity. But the benefits of foreign capital are not an issue in bringing forward this bill. It is not my purpose to deprive Canada of the benefits of foreign capital. This is not a bill to close the door to international investment and turn inwards on ourselves. Quite the contrary. The issue the bill faces is that foreign investment, in addition to its benefits, can also involve costs. A branch plant economy tends to lack the capacity for dynamic innovation-lacks an inner dynamism and outward-looking attitude. It is not necessarily efficient for a $100 billion economy to be designed as a minor replica of a trillion dollar economy.
Our foreign controlled sector is subject to some limitations of research and development, restrictions on export and procurement policies which tie it to international sources of supply at the expense of the stimulation of domestic sources.
We are entering a period in which world demand for our resources will accelerate. We possess a rich and diversified resource base. Our social environment is stable. In the resource area we possess considerable management and technological skills of our own. Given these basic strengths, is it wise for us to let decisions taken abroad in response to foreign needs and priorities determine the rate of extraction of our natural resources and the industrial mix which is likely to result? Does the government not have a responsibility to ensure that development takes place in accordance with Canadian needs and objectives?

The existence of restrictions on research and development, exports and procurement, suggests that scope for increasing benefits exists. Some of these restrictions may reflect basic comparative costs but others are arbitrary and should be removed.
The scope for increasing benefits will vary from industry to industry and from case to case. It is probably greatest in the resource-based industries where the advantage, the location of the resource, is in Canadian hands. Although it is unlikely we can change, in the short run, the location of many processing and fabricating facilities, we may in future be in a position to secure expansion in Canada rather than outside Canada. In the manufacturing sector our main advantage lies in a small but affluent market, a skilled labour force, a relative wage advantage over some countries and a stable political environment. When pressed, they retreat behind a smokescreen of vague generalities, scattering the ground around them with pious statements of intent. They call for effective guidelines for foreign corporations. That is one of the phrases they use. But what guidelines, and for what corporations? They stress the need for more key sectors. But which key sectors are key? And how would they be defined? How much should they be protected? Liberal governments have protected key sectors in the past, but we now see that more comprehensive measures are called for.
Let me explain in more detail why this government decided that the delineation of further key sectors was inappropriate as a general policy response at this time to foreign investment-something that I think some Conservative spokesmen have advocated. Many key sectors in

the so-called commanding heights of the economy have already been protected in a regulatory way. I refer to our legislation in the fields of financial institutions, banks, life insurance companies, trust and loan companies, broadcasting, newspapers and periodicals.

The major areas of the economy where foreign direct investment is unregulated are the manufacturing and resource sectors. How are we to determine which industries in these sectors are most important? What criteria should we use to determine the key or critical sectors that should be protected? Should it be the high technology industries? But technology is not restricted to any one sector. Are we to say that a moribund electronics plant is more important to the country than an innovative, profitable and competitive clothing manufacturer?
Even if we were able to develop a set of criteria to identify key sectors, there are difficult questions regarding which businesses should be included. Let me take automobiles as an hypothetical example. This illustrates the problem of definition in a key sector, the manufacturing sector and the resource sector. Automobiles could include buses, trucks, snowmobiles, off-road vehicles, tires, car radios, air conditioners and so on. You can expand it into a whole series of related products. Where precisely does one draw the line?
Let us look at some of the other questions related to this key sector idea. What degree of protection should we give a key sector? There are a number of alternatives. We could allow no foreign investment. Assuming that you have been able to define and identify-two quite different things-a key sector, what do you do? Do you allow no foreign investment? In that case, we risk cutting ourselves off from the benefits of technological developments elsewhere. Is this sensible if we regard the sector as important in terms of the achievement of national goals? Do you wipe it out? I do not think so.
Second, should we restrict foreign control of assets in a particular sector? Take, for example, computers. Do you say that no more than 50 per cent of the computer industry should be foreign controlled? Think about that particular principle for a moment. This would mean allocating arbitrarily a certain maximum proportion of an industry to foreign control, a simply horrendous administrative and economic problem.
Third, look again at the question of the key sector. Do we say that in a key sector 51 per cent of the shares of every foreign company must be held by Canadians? However, when the 51 per cent is widely held, control could still lie with the foreigner. Scarce Canadian savings could be dissipated, then, in a number of non-controlling situations, thereby reducing the availability of capital for genuinely Canadian-controlled enterprises. Most of these same arguments with respect to the key sector question apply to

March 30,1973

a policy requiring 51 per cent Canadian ownership in all foreign companies irrespective of the particular sector in which they operate.
In summary, the establishment of mandatory Canadian ownership, either across the board or in particular key sectors, as a general policy is arbitrary, protectionist, and potentially very costly economically. It could discourage needed foreign investment in some areas.
To say, however, that a general key sector policy is not appropriate for Canada at this time does not rule out the identification of further key sectors in future where the circumstances are appropriate. For example, it is conceivable that in some resource industries where Canadians have the technology and managerial capability, where foreign demand assures markets, and where capital is available in Canada or can be readily borrowed abroad, the establishment of another key sector may be feasible.
Some Conservative spokesmen seem to think that the only response to the foreign investment issue is to call for measures to encourage Canadians to invest in Canada.

The heart of the Liberal thrust has been the introduction of positive measures to support Canadian industry, particularly those which demonstrate the capacity, the self-interest and the will to grow. The last parliament saw a number of measures implemented to stimulate Canadian ownership and control. A reduced corporation tax rate of 25 per cent on the first $50,000 of income is available only to Canadian-controlled corporations and must be repaid if the firm is transferred to non-Canadian control. These are, for example, the measures to keep savings in Canada; pension funds must retain 90 per cent of their assets in Canada to avoid paying a penalty special tax of 1 per cent per month on the proportion of their assets abroad in excess of that amount. speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
The positive policies that I have discussed earlier all do their part in promoting Canadian ownership and control, but they do not meet the challenge of other far more powerful centres of economic activity abroad. They do not compensate for the attractiveness to foreign capital of our stable political and social environment, of our skilled labour force and substantial resource base, and, in the case of the United States, for our proximity and cultural similarity. They do not compensate for the dynamic power of the multinational corporation whose activities here may be rational from an over-all international perspective but which may impose avoidable costs on Canada.
Finally, our other policies do not compensate for the imperatives of some foreign governments which have intervened to distort market forces in their own national interest threatening to leave Canada holding the short end of the stick. For example, we have the Japanese policies on trade and investment, the new Australian policies and the Mexican policies on foreign investment which we heard so eloquently described in this chamber today by the President of Mexico, and the screening undertaken by the French and British. Even the United States has its DISC, municipal bonds, uranium embargo and countervailing powers requiring no proof of injury.
Canada, no more than others, can rely passively on the operation of market forces alone to protect our interests. For this reason, past Liberal governments have moved to protect the public interest in relationship to foreign investment. I have already referred to the key sectors established in banking, insurance, life insurance, trust and loan companies, broadcasting, newspapers and periodicals. These are still in effect. Other industries and other enterprises already have substantial government participation, for example, the Canadian Broadcasting Commission, Air Canada, Panarctic, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the CNR.
In other sectors where there is already substantial foreign ownership there is one form or another of public regulation, for example, energy development. The combination of provincial regulations and regulation by the National Energy Board tend to ensure Canadian control over the foreign-controlled firms in this sector and performance in accordance with national objectives.
This bill and the positive policies I have described form part of a coherent set of policies designed to foster the achievement of national goals in general and Canadian economic development in particular. They tie in with the proposed reduction in corporate income taxes, the re-
Foreign Investment Review
examination of competition policy and our effort to promote further trade liberalization. It must not be forgotten that the benefits from investment-both foreign and domestic-are enhanced in a competitive and dynamic economy.
Liberal government policy has been an evolving process. Much has already been done. But we recognize that further steps are needed. We are, therefore, moving forward to the more comprehensive foreign investment policy represented by this bill.
This bill is a major step forward. I regard it as the most important part to date of Canada's developing foreign investment policy. The approach chosen is that of screening. We expect in this way to achieve a foreign investment policy which will give us the benefits of foreign investment and at the same time minimize the costs. This requires flexibility. Screening based on performance criteria gives flexibility. The arbitrary alternative approaches of a discriminatory tax system, or of mandatory Canadian ownership rules either across the board or in numerous key sectors could involve a trade-off of employment, investment and growth, which we want to avoid.
We do not want a foreign investment policy which is a luxury commodity for which other economic benefits are traded off. Our objective is to introduce a policy that will have no adverse impact on employment or investment. On the contrary, we see this policy as a necessity if we are to achieve our long term goals for Canada. We see this as a way of building and creating jobs for Canadians in the years to come.
The government will allow those proposed foreign investments likely to result in significant benefits to Canada. It will be able to negotiate with a foreign investor to up the ante and get a better deal for Canada. But takeovers or the establishment of new foreign-controlled businesses that would not bring significant benefits to Canada will be blocked. The bill will be administered by a separate foreign investment review agency reporting directly to the minister.
In considering whether the foreign investor's proposed investment in a Canadian business brings significant benefits to Canada, five factors will be taken into account. The first factor is the effect of the proposed investment on the level and nature of economic activity in Canada, including employment. The second factor is the degree and significance of participation by Canadians in the business enterprise and in any industry or industries in Canada of which it forms a part. The third factor is the effect of the proposed investment on productivity, industrial efficiency, technological development, product innovation and product variety in Canada. The fourth factor is the effect of the proposed investment on competition within any industry or industries in Canada. The fifth factor is the compatibility of the investment with national industrial and economic policies, including those enunciated by the provinces.
The factors are general. They cover all sectors of the economy, resources and services, as well as manufacturing. They are performance oriented and are designed to increase the efficiency and competitiveness of our econo-

Foreign Investment Review
my, while recognizing that we live in a mutually interdependent world.
The government proposes that the review come into effect in two phases. First to be proclaimed will be the review of foreign takeovers of Canadian firms valued at more than $250,000 in terms of their gross assets or with revenues exceeding $3 million. This will be followed by the screening of the establishment of new businesses by foreigners not already doing business in Canada or the opening of a new business by an existing foreign controlled firm in an unrelated line of activity. Because of the possibility of major enterprises being phased into existence from small beginnings over an extended period of time, there would be no thresholds relating to the establishment of new businesses. Expansion of existing foreign-controlled firms through the creation of related businesses would not be screened. When the new business review is introduced, the thresholds applicable to takeovers will be removed except for the important case of an existing foreign-controlled business operating in Canada that proposes to acquire a related business. This step is required to avoid indirect circumvention through the takeover of an unrelated business below the threshold and subsequently expanding it.
The second phase of the bill is delayed to give the government an opportunity to gain some experience operating the review process with takeovers before this second feature comes into force. More important, it will not come into effect until the provinces have been consulted. This is a major feature of the policy. It is a national policy with provincial consultations as an important part. Even more provincial consultation is provided for in the operation of the bill because one of the criteria is a consideration of provincial industrial and economic policy objectives. Machinery will be needed to achieve this consultation.
In connection with the role of provincial priorities, I would like to assure the House that the bill will not have an adverse impact on regional development. Foreign investment needed for the growth and development of a province is likely to be of significant benefit and would be allowed. On the other hand, this bill is not an instrument of regional development policy. It does not contain the bias which is deliberately built into the policy of regional economic expansion. We will not be directing proposed investments from one part of Canada to another under this proposed act. But the economic realities of the region concerned will be emphasized in meeting national economic goals.
One of the criticisms of the bill with which I would like to deal is the fact that it does not cover the expansion of existing foreign-controlled firms unless, of course, they propose to establish unrelated new businesses. We have refrained from proposing this type of review for a number of reasons. Given the large number of firms that are already foreign controlled in Canada, a review of normal expansion would call for an enormous amount of intervention. I am not prepared to argue that the state should have such sweeping authority over normal private decision making. In addition I think there is a difference in kind between the normal growth which takes place as a business prospers and expands its activity on the one hand, and the opening of unrelated businesses on the

other. It seems to me that there is almost an element of retroactivity in intervening in the process of normal growth.
We recognize that this bill will not directly roll back the present level of foreign control in Canadian industry, but as a long term policy objective it will help, along with the success of other policies designed to foster the development of strong Canadian controlled companies, to increase the proportion of Canadian industry controlled by Canadians.
The review process itself is not indifferent to Canadian ownership. The criterion of significant benefit indicates that this is an important concern. Canadian ownership and control is preferred unless the foreign investor is in a position to make a significant economic contribution which a Canadian cannot make. If we were indifferent, we would allow foreign investment as long as it did not involve any detriment to Canada. This is a very important distinction.
There is another point which underlies the importance we attach to Canadian ownership. In determining whether a proposed investment is of significant benefit to Canada, consideration will be given to the degree and significance of Canadian participation which includes the question of ownership. I do not think, on the ownership side, we can be more direct than that.
Mr. Speaker, let me summarize the main elements of the policy that underlie this bill. Canada continues to recognize that foreign investment has a role to play in Canadian development. Provided it contributes to the realization of Canadian objectives it is welcome. This bill asks parliament to give the government the means to achieve this purpose-to ensure that to the maximum possible extent foreign takeovers and the establishment of new foreign-controlled businesses are of significant benefit to Canada. If they are not, they are blocked.
The review process is a flexible instrument which recognizes that foreign direct investment is a complex of costs and benefits. The choice of this approach to foreign investment reflects the government's determination to avoid a trade-off between jobs, investment and growth on the one hand and greater ownership and control on the other. In recognizing the potential role of foreign investment in the Canadian economy, the government rejects isolationism and protectionism but it seeks a way to ensure that Canada achieves better balanced interdependence.
The foreign investment review bill will have four effects. First, it will provide one more public lever in promoting national economic development. Second, it will help us to obtain better performance from foreign investment in Canada on the basis of the criteria contained in the bill. Third, taken with the rest of the policies in this area, it will tend to arrest and reverse the unacceptable trend toward foreign control of enterprise in Canada. Finally, it will be seen as a useful step in supporting the development of a distinctive Canadian identity.
I mentioned during my remarks that Liberal governments have adopted a two pillar approach. While I have spent most of my time describing the policy which under-
March 30, 1973

lies the review process, this in no sense means that the government does not attach the highest importance to policies to develop Canadian entrepreneurship. That is the first pillar. Indeed, to the extent that Canadians- government, businessmen and labour-are able to develop the ingredients of industrial growth in Canada our need and dependence for foreign direct investment decreases. We shall, therefore, pursue with determination policies supporting the development of Canadian entrepreneurship and business efficiency.
Yet the level of foreign direct investment in Canada- the highest in any industrial country- is of concern to all Canadians. Hence our need for the second pillar to protect the public interest of contemporary Canadians and Canadians yet unborn. This bill contains a reasonable and realistic proposal to help us come to grips with this issue. I hope that members from all parties in this House will give this bill their support.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
It was a disappointing speech-it was almost depressing. The split in the Liberal party on this subject, Mr. Speaker, is obviously much deeper and more serious than was thought. The minister also made it obvious that he, like some other ministers of his government, has not yet read the new Income Tax Act or he would not have made some of the assertions he is making now.
Also, Mr. Speaker, I thought the number of questions the minister asked of the Progressive Conservative party this afternoon gave a clear indication that his pessimism is so deeply rooted that he is practising for his role on this side of the House. Bill C-132, "an act to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons and of the establishment of new businesses in Canada by certain persons", appears to represent the government's total response after five years to the growing problem of foreign ownership and control of Canadian industry and resource development. I wish I could say that the mouse had brought forth a mountain or at least an elephant, but after labouring five years all the mouse has managed to bring forth is another mouse. It is a pitifully inadequate response and demonstrates an abject failure in this regard.
The fact that the problem now exists is accepted by most thoughtful people in Canada. Not everyone agrees of course, and there are some strong regional differences of opinion. It is understandable if those areas of Canada where high chronic unemployment exists place a higher
Foreign Investment Review
priority on the creation of new job opportunities than the nationality of the capital which makes them possible. Consequently, it is a matter of regret to the Conservative party that a bill of this importance to various regions of Canada should be introduced without prior consultation with the provinces. Certainly the provincial governments must now be consulted, and must have an input to the determination of guidelines by which significant benefit is determined. Nothing less will satisfy the diversity of approach which is endemic to Canada.
But on an over-all Canadian basis, some acceptable alternative to the present trend must be found. When we reach the point, as we did in 1968, where 46.9 per cent of our metal fabricating industry, 71.8 per cent of our machinery industry, 86.6 per cent of our transportation equipment industry, 81.5 per cent of our chemical and chemical products industry, and 99.5 per cent of our petroleum and coal products industries, as measured by assets, are owned outside Canada, we are in trouble. Since then the level of foreign ownership has continued to increase. Obviously, something must be done. This leads to agreement with the purpose of Bill C-132 as stated in Clause 2(1) which reads:
This Act is enacted by the Parliament of Canada in recognition by Parliament that the extent to which control of Canadian industry, trade and commerce has become acquired by persons other than Canadians and the effect thereof on the ability of Canadians to maintain effective control over their economic environment is a matter of national concern,-
It is easier to agree with the purpose of the bill, as just stated, than it is on the efficacy of its provisions to meet the need. Basically, Bill C-132 is totally negative in its approach. The minister tried to persuade us this afternoon that the opposite is the case, but he was not convincing. It is another "thou shalt not" added to the tens of thousands which already exist. It states that takeovers will only be permitted and new investment allowed when it can be demonstrated that significant benefit will result. But the determination of significant benefit will be largely subjective. It will depend to a considerable extent on the attitude and approach of the commissioner, the minister and the governor in council. The latter will reflect the opinion of the key members of cabinet or "in group" in control at the time. The extent of the inevitable subjectivity concerns me. I know people who could, and probably would, find significant benefit in any proposal, while others of my acquaintance would find it difficult, if not impossible, to find significant benefit in any proposal from foreigners. Any law which is so dependent in its application on the personality and attitude of the people who administer it as Bill C-132 is almost certain to be bad law.
While Bill C-132, unlike its predecessor, extends the screening process to include new investment as well as takeovers, it pays no heed to the expansion of existing foreign-owned companies in Canada except in respect of entry into new and unrelated business. As the Gray report cited 1969 Statistics showing that of the three ways in which foreign ownership in Canada had increased the most imporant was the expansion of existing foreign-con-trolled enterprises, one must conclude that the intent of

March 30, 1973
Foreign Investment Review
the bill is largely cosmetic. Nevertheless, we are prepared to refer it to the committee, where we think it should be subject to the most minute examination.
Why have we reached the stage where a bill such as this is considered expedient? It is the recognition that policies that have been pursued in the past, which may have been appropriate then, are no longer appropriate to Canadian needs, and that unless there is a massive change in policy soon Canada will recede into an industrial and technological backwater. A brief review brings us to the crossroad.
Dependence upon external sources of capital for financing in periods of heavy investment activity has been characteristic of Canadian development. During the exceptional growth that occurred before World War I, non-resident investment was very high and the main source of that investment was London. However, during the first part of the inter-war period, the United States became the principal source of external capital, and by 1926 the portion of Canada's international debt owned in that country exceeded that owned in Britain. With some interruption during the 1930's, United States investment in Canada continued to increase, particularly after 1947, when the period of intense activity in the petroleum industry got under way.
This transition from Britain to the United States as the major investing country also involved a shift in the major type of investment. Whereas British investment has been primarily portfolio investment in railway and utilities, American investment has been primarily direct investment in other Canadian industries. More than half of the United States investment in Canada at the end of 1967 was accumulated since 1957. At $28,030 million, United States investments in 1967 continued to represent more than three quarters of all non-resident investments in Canada. The main rise in that period occurred in direct investments in companies controlled in the United States, which almost doubled. In the same period, portfolio investments in Canada owned in the United States more than doubled, due mainly to large sales of new issues of securities in that country.
Since 1968, an increasing proportion of the capital requirements of United States affiliates in Canada is being raised on the domestic Canadian market rather than being drawn from the parent concern. This is partly due to the effect of the United States foreign direct investment program which was made mandatory in 1968. Even if this tendency for foreign-owned firms to raise money on the Canadian market rather than from the parent concern continues or even increases in the future, there will not necessarily be corresponding changes in the amount of total foreign investment, for the definition of foreign investment hinges on the nationality of the owner of the capital and not on the nationality of the capital itself.
Direct foreign investment can be fairly viewed as one of the most crucial and most dynamic elements in the postwar evolution of Canadian industry. Its effects have been greatest in the petroleum, natural gas and mining industries, which have absorbed over half the total. But very substantial amounts have gone into major branches of the manufacturing sector, such as pulp and paper, automobiles, chemicals and electrical apparatus. This large-scale financing, though highly significant, does not tell the
[Mr. Hellyer.J
whole story. There have been real benefits from the package of technological skills and markets that came with the investment.
While there has been an important positive aspect to direct foreign investment, there has been a negative side as well. Foreign controlled firms undertake little research and development in Canada. A 1970 Industry, Trade and Commerce report on the 1964-67 operations of 326 foreign controlled firms with assets exceeding $5 million each found that many were spending little or nothing on scientific research and development. Their sales had risen a healthy 35 per cent, from about $15.3 billion to $20.7 billion. But research spending rose from $88 million to only $106 million, an increase of just 18 per cent. In the last year of the survey, the average was $325,000 each, a trivial sum for firms of this size. The survey concluded that nowhere in today's industrial world, where science and technology have superseded financial resources as the principal source of corporate power, is the significance of foreign ownership more apparent than in Canada. The report said that the government faces formidable difficulties in devising a program to counteract the bad effects of foreign investment in Canada.
In addition to the sparse expenditures on research and development and the effect of this on career opportunities in Canada, there are other negative aspects of too much foreign control of Canadian industry. Several instances of refusal to sell to countries when sales to those countries would be contrary to U.S. foreign policy have been documented. I will not repeat them here. Far more serious, at this point in time when restrictions on sales to socialist countries are abating, is the tendency of parent organizations to restrict Canadian branch plants and affiliates from aggressively expanding their export sales. While this is not true in all cases, it applies all too frequently and entails a considerable and serious restriction of freedom in so far as Canadian manufacturing industry is concerned. The latest trade statistics released by Statistics Canada bear testimony to the problem.
If Canada had not reached the stage where we are capable of generating the savings necessary for capital expenditures, our options would be more limited. I think that is an essential difference from our position and that of Mexico, as outlined by the president this morning. Fortunately, we have progressed to the point where we can provide, in the aggregate, our own capital requirements. In their first of a series of studies for the Toronto Stock Exchange examining Canada's capital markets, Professors David Shaw and T. Ross Archibald provide statistical documentation of Canada's sources of capital funds since the end of the second world war.
In 1950, domestic savings accounted for 92 per cent of total capital expenditures while foreign sources financed only about 8 per cent. At that time gross domestic savings equalled 20 per cent of GNP. By 1960, domestic sources declined and provided only 83 per cent of capital formation. Similarly, the rate of domestic savings in 1960 had fallen to 16 per cent of GNP. By 1970, Canadian domestic savings amounted to 23 per cent of GNP and exceeded domestic capital formation so that Canada became a net
March 30, 1973

exporter of $1.1 billion. Consequently, Shaw and Archibald were able to conclude, and I quote:
Canada's historical international position as an importer of funds (had) changed and this country (could now) generate sufficient savings to finance the current level of capital expenditure.
While this is good news, it is necessary to add the caution that a significant proportion of these Canadian savings accrues to foreign controlled companies in Canada. Their retained earnings represent a substantial proportion of the net savings of the corporate sector. One must concur in the conclusion of the Gray report where it states:
Canada's capacity to finance its own future growth does assume a large savings role by foreign controlled companies in Canada.
While it is encouraging to believe that Canada now has the potential to paddle its own canoe to a much greater extent, it is disappointing to conclude that Bill C-132 will not do the job. Greater economic independence is possible and the reasons for seeking it have never been stronger, but something more than Bill C-132 is required.

speechtext:
Step number three would be a gradual but massive increase in the extent of research and development undertaken in Canada. Canadians must come to realize that the development of modern technology requires massive public investment and cannot be left entirely to the vagaries of the marketplace. In 1967, only 18 per cent of research and development spending by Canadian firms was financed out of public funds; in the United States 53 per cent of research and development spending by private firms was government-financed, while comparable figures for the United Kingdom and France were 35 per cent and 42 per cent respectively.
The United States government financed the development of the first U.S. computer, the Univac model by Remington-Rand, as a naval fire-control device, and the first IBM models for the DEW line. The formation of International Computers Limited in the United Kingdom

was backed by the U.K. government to the extent of an $8.4 million equity position and $32.3 million in research and development funds in 1968.
Canada lost out in this race even though we were at one time on the cutting edge of technology. In the 1950s and early 1960s, British-owned Ferranti-Packard Limited of Toronto developed a series of advanced computers beginning with the Datar, a naval operations control system, and climaxing in the FP 6000 which was a resounding technological and commercial success. But after making four of the units, Ferranti-Packard ran out of funds and, since British capital exports to dollar nations are subject to foreign exchange controls, was unable to draw more financing from the parent firm.
Consequently, the computer designs and technology were sold to another British firm which has since become International Computers Limited. The FP 6000 evolved into the ICL series, of which 1,500 had been sold by the beginning of 1970. With the Canadian development start, ICL gained 43 per cent of the British market for computers, compared to only 30 per cent for IBM, making Britain the only market in the west where IBM is not the major seller of computers. By 1970, ICL had sold 47 installations in the Soviet Union and other eastern bloc nations, for $35 million, making it the largest seller of computers to eastern Europe.
Professor Arthur Porter, head of the team which designed the Datar computer, told the Special Senate Committee on Science Policy:
Canada made a tremendous breakthrough in information technology ... I believe Canada was the first nation to set up three individual data-handling systems and to tie them together over radio links
He said Britain's ICL computer series could be said to have been "conceived and designed in Canada".
We were ahead. We were not only ahead in interactive computer systems, but we were ahead in modular solid state computer technology, which is the basis of the modern computer.
Canada can compete in research and development, but must have the ownership, control and follow-through to capitalize on early advantages. In this, as in so many other cases, that important early lead was lost.
There are, fortunately, some happier examples. One is Northern Electric, a major Canadian producer of telephone equipment. This corporation provides us with an illustration of how a Canadian subsidiary can succeed after its ties with its U.S. parent have been severed. Ironically, the cutting of the umbilical cord was due to American rather than Canadian policy. The abandoned baby survived and thrived. From its inception, in 1895, to 1956 the corporation did very little of its own research and development. Instead, it manufactured products designed in the United States by its parent corporation, Western Electric. In 1956, however, U.S. anti-trust legislation forced the parent to divest itself of its control over the Canadian subsidiary.
Since that time, the Canadian corporation has transformed itself from an importer and purchaser of technology to a producer and exporter of technology. Recent statistics bear this out. In 1960, 90 per cent of its designs came from foreign sources, but by 1970 only 19 per cent of its designs came from foreign sources. In the same period,
March 30, 1973

its own designs rose from 5 per cent to 80 per cent, with about 20 per cent being hybrids of domestic and foreign work. Professional staff rose from three in 1967 to 727 in
1969.	Total R and D staff increased from 153 in 1960 to more than 2,000 in 1970. The research and development budget went from $2.6 million in 1960 to $37.7 million in
1970.	This represented an increase in research and development, as a percentage of sales, from 1.5 per cent to 8.2 per cent.
Since its Canadianization, Northern Electric has also helped to strengthen Canada's balance of trade by expanding exports and displacing imports. Export sales rose from 2.5 per cent of its total sales in 1963 to 17.9 per cent in 1970. Between 1958 and 1968, the percentage of sophisticated components from Canadian sources rose from 62 per cent to 85 per cent.

This corporation has had an extensive research and development program since as long ago as 1965 when its research and development budget amounted to 3.3 per cent of its sales, or $940,000. Surely, then, these two success examples of Canadian corporations demonstrate what a manufacturer can achieve through greater research and development and aggressive management and, conversely, what a manufacturer can lose through lack of its own research and development because of non-resident control.
Canadians can do it if given the chance. These two untypical examples should become the norm. Canadian-owned corporations should be given preference in research and development funds, but incentive should also be provided to foreign-owned corporations willing to expand their research and development facilities in Canada and to develop products for export markets. The aim of Canadian research and development policy should be the employment of Canadian scientists, engineers and product planners in the development of a capability which, proportionately to our resources, is second to none on earth.
Step number four is the development of more flexibility in our financial institutions in order to cope with our policy objectives. Although, as I indicated earlier, Canada has sufficient funds to finance current investment
Foreign Investment Review
requirements, the allocative functions of Canadian capital markets leave much to be desired. This is true both nationally and regionally. We have not yet mastered the technique of matching the entrepreneur and the capital he requires at the proper time.
There is a desperate need in Canada for the creation of new institutions or the expansion of existing ones to supply more venture capital. We must expand, dramatically, our capability to assemble the financing and all the other elements required to establish a new domestic enterprise or to acquire control of an existing foreign-owned enterprise with substantial assets and activities in Canada.
Canadians often feel, with justification, that it is easier for a foreign-owned corporation to get a loan from a Canadian bank than for a Canadian entrepreneur.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Indeed, our banking system has performed a considerable disservice to Canada by financing the takeover of Canadian industries by foreigners. They must change their policies and make Canadian credit readily available to Canadians, even if that involves some small risk. The chartered banks, acting collectively, should be encouraged to form one or more subsidiaries specializing in merchant banking and venture capital. Insurance companies and pension funds should be encouraged to mobilize funds for similar purposes and to form syndicates to permit sufficient diversity to spread the risks associated with venture capital investment. The role of the Industrial Development Bank should also be expanded to increase substantially its capability and, hopefully, its daring. It could play a much more dynamic role, especially in the alleviation of regional disparity.
If anyone doubts the necessity for major change they need only look at the present situation. An oil refinery is to be built in Newfoundland. It will be equipped with British machinery, financed by British capital and, of course, owned in the United States. The Canadian government and Canadian institutions either could not or would not help. Canada can support development for the people of Tanzania, Algeria and Chile, but not for the people of Newfoundland. While the former may be desirable, surely we should also be able to support at the same time our own growth and development.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
It is quite obvious that Canadian financial institutions, if the chartered banks are included, have the financial ability to mobilize the vast sums of venture capital required. A very significant reorganization will be required, however, together with a change in outlook in tune with the times and cognizant of Canada's real industrial needs. Canada desperately needs a renaissance of entrepreneurship in its business community. Without the vision and initiative that only gifted entrepreneurs can bring to a nation's economy, Canada will remain locked into the secondary roles offered by the head offices of large, multinational enterprises. However, if the nation's imagination responds to the entrepreneurial instinct

March 30, 1973
Foreign Investment Review
latent in Canada, we could develop into an innovative country imbibed with a sense of initiative and achievement.
Step number five, Mr. Speaker, is to combine all of these ingredients into a massive effort to increase Canadian exports. We must remember that success goes to the commercially adept and not just to the technically brilliant. Our managerial skills must be put to work and developed. The objective would be not just a balance of transactions on current account but a substantial surplus. The surplus would not be allowed to accumulate, however, and add to our already swollen reserves of United States' dollars. An equivalent amount would be used to purchase equities and reduce our foreign indebtedness. In other words, we would acquire ownership and control of major companies with substantial assets and activities in Canada.
The objective of this strategy would be a gradual but significant shift in ownership. A 20 per cent reduction in foreign ownership in a ten-year period would not be an unrealistic goal. We would attempt, over a period of years, to achieve Canadian ownership and control of giant, multinational enterprises in such industries as electronics, rubber, chemicals, transport equipment, etc. The list would include each field of endeavour that is important to us and which offered a reward commensurate with the investment we would be required to make. The President of Mexico said this morning that the question is of decisive importance. The future of Canada's independence of action is at stake. These industries would not be government-owned; they would be Canadian-owried, with the widest possible equity participation both directly by individuals and through mutual and pension funds. Their acquisition and development would be a team effort by Canadian entrepreneurs and Canadian financial institutions with the encouragement and assistance of the government and the people of Canada.
This positive, Progressive Conservative strategy represents a positive approach to a serious problem. It recognizes that in a world of giants, the benefits of independence go only to those who are giants. That is not to say that small business will be less important. Quite the contrary; small business will benefit from the extra thrust and by the enlarged requirement for Canadian sourcing of sophisticated components and products of all kinds. The emphasis on giants is merely recognition that Canadians should not be limited to small business but should have access to the major league as well. Only a strong and mature economic and industrial base will give Canada the capacity to retain and expand its position in world markets. To achieve that level of economic competence, Canada must develop internally that pinnacle of technological expertise which is a prerequisite for an innovative and dynamic economic structure.
Can we do it? Of course we can. It is just the kind of challenge young Canadians want and need. In closing, I would like to borrow a phrase I believe to be appropriate: Make no small plans for they hold no fire to stir men's blood.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, my colleagues and I in the New Democratic Party throughout the country have for many years

expressed concern about the extent of foreign ownership of the economy in Canada and about the trends that have continued throughout the years. I must begin this afternoon by saying to you, Mr. Speaker, that as I listened to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), and later to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), I continued to feel sad for my country as far as its economic independence is concerned.
The minister, who really ought not to have done so, boasted about the steps that have been taken by Liberal governments. It is not until now that this government has come to realize that the question of Canadian economic independence is an important one, that Canadian economic independence is being demanded by ever-increasing numbers of Canadians. Only now has the government begun to realize that fact. While the minister boasted about the tiny, mincing steps that have been taken through the years, the situation is really rather shameful since they did not accomplish anything, and could not accomplish anything as far as the major problem of the control of Canada's economy is concerned. Nor should the minister have boasted about his bill, though I detected in his speech the realization that Bill C-132 was merely one step, and perhaps not a very large one, in the direction that he claims we want to go.
We then heard the hon. member for Trinity, who spoke vigorously and held out, he said, promises of a positive and dynamic policy. But analyse that policy, Mr. Speaker, and all it amounts to at every turn is further tax concessions to the corporations, additional tax concessions to the wealthy investors, more tax concessions to those who will build, he says, Canadian entrepreneurship-everything at the expense of the Canadian people. When the hon. member talked of further and massive progress in research and development in this country, what did he really say? He chided the Canadian government for the fact that only 18 per cent-I think that was the figure-of public money has gone into research and development in Canada, whereas 53 per cent has been spent in the United States.
What the hon. member is saying to this parliament and to the people of Canada is that most of the corporations of this country in these fields which are foreign owned should be given millions of dollars of Canadian taxpayers' money to carry on research and development in Canada. Those were his solution to the problems of Canadian economic independence. He suggested greater tax concessions for the wealthy, the rich and the powerful corporations.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
The hon. member can say "nonsense" as long as he likes, but that is exactly what the hon. member for Trinity said. He criticized the small capital gains tax we have in this country and all the other little measures we have undertaken to close some of the loopholes. He wants more tax concessions for investors and more tax concessions for corporations. That is one way, he says, in which we are able to carry out research and development in this country. He says the federal treasury should not put in 18 per cent of what is now being spent on research and
March 30,1973

development, but 53 per cent. That is exactly what the Conservative party is proposing.
In that respect the Liberals and Conservatives are clearly one. The only way they can see of promoting the economy of Canada is to make the wealthy wealthier and the powerful more powerful, all at the expense of the ordinary Canadian worker and the small Canadian businessman. We reject that kind of approach to Canada's economy and Canadian economic independence.
The hon. member for Trinity said-and this is the kind of statement that is so often made by Tories, particularly in this parliament, which lowers my respect for them- that if you have a screening agency, the decisions will be subjective. I should like to know what, in heaven's name, he means. I should like to know what agency, what board, what minister or what other organization you may have for making decisions in other than a subjective way.
My criticism of the bill is very considerable. I will come to that in a moment. I want to add at this point that I reject the dogmatic position of the Conservative party as an alternative to the bill before us, because in my opinion it is not an alternative; it is merely a continuation of the policy which has been followed until now. The minister was right when he said that a successful, profitable Canadian company is obviously a very attractive firm for foreign takeover. That is what has happened in the past and that is what will happen in the future.
We consider the discussion on this bill as being of immense importance to this parliament and this country. I am grateful for the statement by the President of Mexico to the Parliament of Canada this day. As I listened to him, I was both grateful for his eloquence and appreciative of his statements, and at the same time ashamed for my country. Mexico is a country much weaker than Canada, with fewer resources, much more dependent upon the outside world, and with a history of violence. But Mexico has gained its independence. It is a country that had the courage to nationalize the oil industry, taking it out of the hands of foreign corporations and putting it into the hands of the people of Mexico.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
It did so despite the history of relations with the United States, which might have involved a great deal of fear about the things that might happen. Mexico has had a history of relations with the United States which has not been as peaceful as ours since 1812. Their history being different. One might have expected the government and the people of Mexico, having had this experience of U.S. forceful intervention, to have hesitated in taking steps against the American-owned oil corporations in Mexico. But that country had the wisdom to recognize the importance of this industry to their economic independence, and the courage to act upon it. They did not stop there: they went on to further measures which have just been introduced and about which His Excellency spoke this morning.
The President of Mexico said last night, and this morning, that his government intends to adopt further measures to reduce holdings of foreign corporations in that country's economy. I said that as I listened to the Presi-
Old Age Security
dent I was proud to be associated with him in this House, but at the same time I was ashamed at the timidity which Canada has shown throughout the years. I was ashamed by the fears which Liberals and Conservatives have shown, and particularly about the way Canadian business leaders have been prepared to sell off Canada's wealth to multinational corporations because they could make an easier and faster buck.
We are not concerned about Canadian economic independence on the basis of some arid or negative kind of nationalism. This is not because Canadian corporations are any more thoughtful of workers or consumers than foreign-owned corporations might be. The objectives of a corporation, whatever its ownership, are the same. The interest in profit and power is the same. The public interest takes second place whether the corporation is privately owned by Canadians, owned by Americans or owned by nationals of any other country.
Our concern is not in respect of this question concerning Canadian economic independence. Our concern is in respect of the question regarding the future of this country being decided by forces outside which we cannot even influence. Our concern is for the future of jobs for Canadian workers. We are concerned with the fact that these jobs are often is jeopardy as a result of a branch plant economy. We are concerned about a resource industry which yanks the wealth out of the ground and ships it away as quickly as possible, without taking the trouble to process, refine or develop it by employing Canadian workers in Canada. These are the things that worry us. Above all, we are concerned because history has taught us that a country which does not control its own economic destiny is unable to control its own political and social destiny.
If it is our intention to go on with private members' hour at four o'clock, as is usual on Friday, this might be a good point for me to finish my remarks, Mr. Speaker.
