speakeroldname: Mr. Robert C. Coates (Cumberland-Colchester North) moved:
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED GUARANTEED INCOME PAYABLE TO MARRIED COUPLES WHEN EITHER SPOUSE REACHES AGE 65
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give immediate consideration to the establishment of a program, in conjunction with the provinces, that would guarantee a basic income to a man and wife, upon one or the other attaining age 65, of not less than that amount they would qualify to receive under present federal legislation, were both to have attained age 65 on the date one or the other attained that age.

March 30, 1973
Old Age Security
He said: Mr. Speaker, I embark upon the debate of this private members' notice of motion with a degree of optimism that certainly did not exist prior to October 30, 1972. I do so for two reasons. First, there is no doubt that a government, whatever government it might be, which finds itself in a minority position in this chamber indicates a degree of sensitivity for the problems of people which does not exist when a government holds a majority position in the House.
Second, I take this approach because of the activities and the statements of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). He is new to this House but is not new to this government, bearing in mind that for a number of years he sat in the back room conceiving policy for the government. For a number of years he has made a contribution to one government after another, as a bureaucrat. I may say it has come as a pleasant surprise to me and, I am sure, to many Canadians, especially those who are affected by social justice legislation, that the new minister has grasped, in the way he has, the responsibility associated with his portfolio. My only concern is whether the minister can translate into action the words he has spoken about social justice.
I feel more confident about his ability to do so because he has been a bureaucrat for a very long time. If anyone should be able to cut the red tape associated with federal bureaucracy, it should be him. I say this because I have read very carefully the many statements the minister has made, and I agree with most of them.
There is an unbelievable morass associated with social justice which must be straightened out. I do not know whether the end result should be a guaranteed annual income or some other program that would eliminate the duplication and, I hope, much of the heavy burden of cost associated with many of the problems relating to the minister's department.
The legislation which has been introduced relating to social justice is important. At the same time, however, far too much money is being spent on administration. In too many instances, federally, provincially and municipally, the people affected by social justice programs and the problems associated with them are not receiving sufficient income to maintain themselves with dignity.
I was very pleased to read the minister's comments regarding the social assistance programs which exist in many of the provinces. I agree with him that too many people who must rely on assistance associated with the Canada Assistance Program are not receiving as much money as our old age pensioners. These people face a terrible burderi, especially when the breadwinner is disabled and there is a family of anywhere up to ten persons dependent upon a cheque from the provincial government that does not provide them with sufficient income on which to exist. But that is the case. It is the case in the province of Nova Scotia where until recently, when amendments were proposed to the act, a disabled person, his wife and family had to exist on $200 a month. That was a scandalous situation.
My motion relates to another unfortunate situation affecting a great many older Canadians. I refer to a situa-

tion in which a man and his wife, or a wife and her husband, endeavour to maintain themselves on what is available to them through one cheque for old age pension and the guaranteed income supplement. I wish to place on record a few of the letters I have received from constituents. These letters bring the point very much to mind. They are all of recent date and come from various areas of my constituency. I am sure this indicates that if people were writing me from all across Canada, the letters would contain the same type of wording. This situation exists wherever there are older people and it is a situation we must eliminate. This letter comes from Oxford, in my constituency, and is from a lady who writes:
I am writing to state I think the old age pension should be dropped to age 60 years. For instance, my husband gets the old age security pension, and I am not old enough for this by several years. And by the time we pay electricity, fuel, groceries and medicine there just isn't enough to go around. I am also diabetic and should be buying special foods without sugar, etc.
I wonder if the government thinks that I should starve or do without the necessities of life.
That letter is dated January 25, 1973. The next letter is from Parrsboro, which is quite a distance from Oxford, and is dated January 25, 1973. It reads:
I am writing to ask if there is anything that can be done to help us. My husband is an old age pensioner, but I am not old enough to get the pension and I am unable to go out to work. What with the cost of living going up, so also the cost of medicines, we just can't have the things which we need. We both have to take some medicine, not as much as some people, thank goodness for that, but even so we can't always get the medicine we need.
My husband gets a small Canada pension each month, which gives him a total of $174.28 a month, which doesn't go very far with the cost of living so high.
Here we have two people who are trying to live on $174 a month. The position in which these people find themselves is scandalous. It is caused by the situation which exists at the present time. Here is another letter from Springhill:
If I may take a few minutes of your valuable time and express my views regarding old age pensions and unemployment insurance; in regards to pensions, in the majority of cases the wife is five to ten years younger than her husband, which means he cannot afford to retire at age 65 on one pension due to cost of living, taxes, etc., and due to the fact that older people seem to require more drugs and medicines.
I will be 67 next birthday and can see no way that I can retire before reaching 69 or 70, due to the fact that my wife is six years younger than me and does require continual medical care. So I think that the wives of older husbands should be given the pension when their husbands reach age 65, instead of putting millions of dollars into unemployment insurance. Let the younger men go to work. Instead, we are building a country of soft young men.
The next letter I wish to quote is from Amherst and reads:
My family and I have given you support before in elections and will again if you can possibly help me any in receiving a pension. I was 60 years of age on September 13, 1972. My husband receives the 65-year old pension and it is not enough for both of us. He only receives $84 a month and it don't even commence to pay the bills; there is nothing for medicines and clothes.
Here is another letter, from Joggins. It reads:
I am writing this letter to see if you can help us.
March 30, 1973

Mr. Brown is 71 years old and I am 64 years old. Mr. Brown is getting the old age pension, $150, and I get a small $46 cheque from the welfare. We have rent to pay, electric bills, coal bills, groceries bills and doctor's bills and medication bills, and have to hire someone to do the housework. At times Mr. Brown has amnesia and I have heart trouble and arthritis.
This is the sad situation in which a great many people of this country find themselves: one of the two spouses qualifies for old age security, and the two of them try to survive together until the other one qualifies for old age security. There is no reason why we cannot work out a scheme whereby when the breadwinner reaches the qualifying age for old age security, the other spouse will qualify for an equivalent amount, so that at least the two people can have a decent amount of money available to them.
A great many of these cases would be eliminated if we were to drop the age of eligibility for old age security benefits from 65 to 60 years of age. I realize the cost would be great. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said it would cost $1.1 billion. First of all, I do not think that that is too high a price to pay to ensure that our elderly people receive a decent amount of money, in a nation as affluent as ours. Second, I think there are systems which would allow us to do it gradually, in the same way as when we reduced the age of eligibility for old age security from 70 to 65.
I am informed that the total number of males in Canada between the age of 60 and 64 is 381,690, and the total number of females in the same age bracket is 395,320. This gives a total of 777,010. I feel that over a five-year period, a program could be implemented that would eliminate the problem that I am bringing to the attention of the House and also reduce the age requirement for old age security. This would do two things: first, it would eliminate this problem, which is a very real and severe one, faced by many Canadians; second, it would allow a great many people to remove themselves from the labour force at a time when we have high unemployment and it would allow younger people to move into the labour force.
This would accomplish two things: it would ensure that people could retire when they desired to do so; and, second, it would provide an income for people which would at least provide them with the necessities of life, which a great many of them do not receive at present under this system. It would also eliminate some of the older people from the labour force by allowing them to retire when they desire to do so, and provide opportunities for younger people to move in and take their place.
In this way the government would achieve two things: first, it would ensure that older citizens who have contributed so much to the building of this nation would receive a decent income on retirement; and, second, it would provide further opportunities for younger people who desire jobs but cannot find them now.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED GUARANTEED INCOME PAYABLE TO MARRIED COUPLES WHEN EITHER SPOUSE REACHES AGE 65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read with great interest the motion before the house. The hon. member proposes:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give immediate consideration to the establishment of a programme, in conjunction with the provinces, that would guarantee a basic
Old Age Security
income to a man and wife, upon one or the other attaining age sixty-five, of not less than that amount they would qualify to receive under present federal legislation, were both to have attained age sixty-five on the date one or the other attained that age.
Mr. Speaker, the welfare of our fellow citizens who have reached the golden age is a subject close to my heart. I was reading recently in a Statistics Canada publication that we are happy to number among the people of Canada more than 1,744,000 Canadians aged 65 or over. Among these are men and women who did their share to build this Canada we are proud of, men and women who still contribute to the welfare of the society they live in men and women who face their golden days with confidence, with serenity.
Mr. Speaker, it is undeniable that the recent changes to the Old Age Security Act proposed in the House by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) are a source of great progress, a progress which will allow a greater number of our fellow citizens aged 65 or over to face the future with confidence and serenity.
When we look at the history of this programme, since its implementation, we can notice this progress.

Twenty-five years ago, the only payment available for senior citizens was the universal old age security benefit, which amounted at that time to $40 a month. In 1957, that payment amounted to $46 a month starting at the age of 70. Between 1957 and 1962, when the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was prime minister of this country, the benefit was increased by $9 during the first part of the Conservative administration and by $10 toward the end of their administration.
Successive Liberal governments have raised the benefits available to pensioners on eight occasions since that time. In 1963, during the stewardship of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, the old age pension was raised to $75 a month. A 2 per cent escalation clause to offset the cost of living was introduced in 1966. In 1970, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the pension was set at $80 a month and became payable to persons aged 65 and over as a result of action taken in 1966. In 1972, the Liberal government introduced an escalation clause to fully adjust the old age pension to increases in the cost of living, and during the budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) announced that as of April 1, 1973, the basic old age pension would be increased to $100 a month.
Ten years ago there was no income supplement for senior citizens who had no other source of revenue aside from the old age pension. The guaranteed income supplement was introduced in 1966 and provided a maximum payment of $30 a month above the old age pension to pensioners with no other income. In 1970, the maximum supplement was increased to $55. In 1972, the government under the present Prime Minister increased the maximum to $67.12 per month and indexed the guaranteed income supplement to fully reflect increased in the cost of living. Canadians over 65 years of age were eligible, before the recent amendments to the Old Age Security Act were introduced, to receive a basic old age pension of $82.88 a

March 30, 1973
Old Age Security
month and a maximum supplement of $67.12, depending on the level of their income.
As of April 1, 1973, taking into account the measures enacted under the Old Age Security Act, the basic pension of $100 a month, added to the newly-indexed supplement of $70.14, will mean an income of $170 a month for a single Canadian over 65 who has no other income. In the case of a married couple both of whom are over 65, the maximum benefit payable will be $325.

Mr. Speaker, it is to the credit of the Canadian parliament that it has always taken a keen interest in the problems of those of our citizens who have reached the normal retiring age of 65. I therefore consider that the matter before us today deserves our thorough attention.
Mr. Speaker, I have never been one to oppose reform or progress simply because it is piecemeal rather than universal. There is no shortage of excuses for stagnation. In my opinion, it is better to improve the financial condition of certain groups, when we can afford to, than to do nothing. Nevertheless, we must be aware of what we are doing, and make sure that public funds will be spent in the best way possible. This is an area in which the federal and provincial governments have responsibilities in common, and must act together as far as they can.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, that the provincial governments have a very special responsibility to those under 65, by virtue of their various social welfare programs. The federal government contributes enormously to the social welfare programs that the provinces devise and administer. Under the Canada Assistance Plan adopted by the federal government, 50 per cent of payments made by provincial governments to people in need are taken from funds voted by parliament.
Some will say-and often rightly-that a couple in which one of the partners reaches 65 may need special assistance. We must not, however, forget that people under 65, whether single or married, may also be in need. The answer of course is not easy. It is true that those people under 65 come under provincial social assistance programs. For those people, particularly those who are incapable of working, there is sometimes a considerable gap between what they can get under the provincial plans and what they could get under the federal old age security plan.
I fully agree, Mr. Speaker, that we must give additional help to those people but I think that the solution to this problem lies in the guidelines contained in the Speech from the Throne and the authoritative speeches made in this House on January 11 and March 1st by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). Those problems can only be resolved through close co-operation with the provinces and the integration of security plans but I think, Mr. Speaker, that a couple where one of the spouses, particularly the spouse who is the breadwinner of the family and who reaches the age of 65, generally faces the same problem as the family where both spouses have reached the age of 65. Nevertheless they come under different plans.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the government should look further into that in co-operation with the provinces so that

we, as parliamentarians, can know clearly and exactly what is the plight of those families and act with full knowledge of the facts.
The blue book introduced in 1970 by the predecessor of the Minister of National Health and Welfare said, and I quote:
More than 800,000 aged persons over 65 have such low incomes that they qualify for the income supplement.
Among those, Mr. Speaker, we find of course married people where one of the spouses is under 65. If it is true that the eradication of poverty depends basically on the strength of the private sector of the economy as well as on the efficiency of government measures for growth and stability, nevertheless the fact remains that our fellow citizens aged over 65 can benefit from them only through an act of parliament.
The case of the family whose main provider has reached the age of 65 ought to concern us just as much as that of the family where both spouses have reached that age. The problems are the same and perhaps the solutions should also be the same.
Mr. Speaker, it is too easy to succumb to the temptation of playing politics in that field. Why not bid higher than the other guy? Why not gain temporary popularity by promising favours to certain categories of people? But a government, a parliament that is aware of its responsibilities must study the possibilities of extending them to the other categories as well if it wants to reach enlightened conclusions. To set new priorities without first clearly identifying them with the provincial authorities would not serve the true interests of the Canadian people.
Speaking in the debate on the throne speech on January 11, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) said there ought to be a review also of the whole of Canada's social security system. The minister also proposed a framework within which this review could be carried out. The five-point framework is built around the following principles. First, the social security plan shall ensure to persons unable to work, the elderly, the blind and the disabled, an annual guaranteed income that is fair and compassionate; second, the social security system applicable to persons able to work shall include incentives and emphasize the need for reinstatement of social welfare recipients into the labour force; third, a just ratio must be maintained between the income of workers who earn only the minimum wage or not much more, the guaranteed income of those unfit to work and the allowances paid to persons able to work but temporarily unemployed; fourth, the provinces may wish to have a social security system modified in accordance with tlpe social needs, the income level and the cost of living within their jurisdiction; fifth, the reappraisal of Canada's social security system must be conducted jointly by the federal government and the provinces.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the best method of fighting poverty in this country is through the creation of meaningful jobs which take people off the welfare rolls. There will always be citizens, however, who for one reason or another, in temporary or special circumstances, are

unable to work. To give a few examples, there are in this country 150,000 abandoned mothers who must take care of 350,000 children; 200,000 disabled people between the ages of 18 and 65. Furthermore, some families would certainly welcome increases in the family allowance.
There are some of the reasons why I believe we must undertake a complete review of present social security legislation. Our reserves are not unlimited; therefore, our priorities must be clearly set out. Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people and this parliament will follow very closely the discussions between the federal minister and the provincial ministers of health and welfare. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates), as I would commend any member of any party of this House, on raising the question of lowering the pensionable age. The hon. member who has proposed this motion has suggested in it just one means of achieving that object, namely, lowering the pensionable age, and that is by providing the pension to the spouse of a pensioner where that spouse has not yet reached the age of 65. I believe he will agree that this is a step in the direction of what he really wants to achieve, and not only am I completely with him in what he wants to achieve, but I have the same notice of motion on the order paper and I think I have had something to say about it on a number of occasions.
I say to the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Mon-tagnes (Mr. Fox) that this is not exactly a time for boasting over what his party has done over the years, all of which has been provided. Some of us could recount the story in our sleep, having heard it so often. Indeed, I have lived through all of it. Nor is it a time to push off the issue by saying it has to be studied in depth in the context of the whole of our social security problem. I do not think there is any question but if that mythical thing, a free vote, could take place in this House so that members could express the views that are being expressed to them by their constituents, there would be wide support in all parts of the House for immediate action to lower the eligible age.
One of the reasons I am glad the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North was in a position to proceed with this motion this afternoon is that this is the very week in which we have given third and final reading to one bill respecting the Old Age Security Act-we passed it a couple of days ago-providing for an increase in the basic amount of the pension to $100 a month. I was disappointed, when that bill was brought in, that it did not do something about lowering the eligible age as well.
I remind hon. members that the general practice around here is to be satisfied if an act is amended once a session, but I hope this House does not feel that way about the Old Age Security Act. It will not be enough just to coast along on the knowledge that the pension was raised in the present session to $100 a month. The issue of people under 65 particularly those who have been referred to this afternoon, namely, spouses of pensioners on a pension-the
Old Age Security
result being that two people are having to live on a pension for one-is one that must be resolved.
I say to my hon. friend who has sponsored this motion that although I support him in this as an initial step, I am sure he will agree with me that if we provided pensions for younger spouses, we would immediately be faced with the problems of widows below the age of 65 and of spinsters below that age who would say that if certain people are getting the pension, why should they not get it? The real answer to this problem-and I give the hon. member full marks for referring to it in his speech today-is to lower the pensionable age to 60. I urge that this be done, not only with respect to the Old Age Security Act but also with respect to the Canada Pension Plan.
I support those who contend that we would make a significant contribution to our unemployment problem if we could make it possible for people over 60 to retire, because then there would be more jobs for younger people. But there will not be sufficient inducement for people to retire at age 60 if all they will then get is the old age security pension. In addition to the old age security pension, they must also be given the Canada Pension Plan benefit. We must also develop a climate in which industrial pensions are made available at age 60.
I believe that is one of the next important reforms that we must now make in old age security. We have made many reforms over the years, as hon. members know. My connection with old age pensions began in the days when it was $20 a month at age 70, with a means test. Now the age has been reduced to 65, and for the larger part of the pension we have got rid of the means test. We also have an escalation clause in our pension legislation. I think we must improve that escalation clause and provide for an escalation not just equal to the rise in the cost of living, but for one equal to the rise in the standard of living.
The other point that is before us this afternoon, in my view, is an extremely important one and I want to see it resolved in the present session. I want to see a break in the age 65 floor. I know that this view is not held just by members of my party; it is held by members of the Conservative party, and my friends across the way in the Social Credit party also hold this view strongly. To my knowledge, there are scads of members in the Liberal party who feel the same way.
So I hope we will not just have discussions like the one we are having today; that we will not just have a valuable discussion in the Standing Committee on Health, Wealth and Social Affairs and a discussion with the provinces: I hope the government realizes that it will be bombarded with demands on this issue throughout the session and that what we really want is another bill amending the Old Age Security Act in the present session of parliament. That bill must provide for pensions to be made payable to spouses who are below 65 when the breadwinner is a pensioner. Preferably, pensions should be made payable across the board, right now, at age 60.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to congratulate the hon. member for Cumberland-

March 30, 1973

Colchester North (Mr. Coates) for having introduced a motion which reads in part as follows:
The government should give immediate consideration to the establishment of a program, in conjunction with the provinces, that would guarantee a basic income to a man and wife, upon one or the other attaining age sixty-five-
One could say in the future, I hope, "the pensionable age". I am sorry that this private members' hour does not allow us to achieve positive actions and I have always hated that period which means nothing. We talk during one hour, everybody expresses good wishes, but by the end, the bill is talked out and its study is put off until the twelfth of never. Tonight, I hope we end our remarks before five o'clock in order, at least, to have the motion voted on. However, I am afraid that, as usual, the question will fizzle out.
For years, we have been asking for an equal pension for the spouse having not yet reached the pensionable age when the husband has become eligible.
In fact, in 1966, my colleague from Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) introduced a similar motion; as can be seen, the question is not new but it still took us six years to convince the members of the Conservative party, and we still hope that the Liberals also will finally give their agreement.
Six years is a long period for the older people-and perhaps are they to wait another six months or another year-to get at last a favourable reply to a request that the whole population has put before the governments in all provinces.
What is new today is the progress the idea has made, although a difficult one, but we have scored marks.
In the fight we put up on March 27 and 28, we obtained the support of the New Democratic Party. I have just heard the speech of that party's spokesman and I was happy to note that the New Democratic Party is unanimous on this matter, as could be expected from their statement, as today I feel one cannot rely on the statement of one individual but must know the opinion of each and every one. At any rate, they even congratulated us on putting up this fight, which opened the eyes of many hon. members.
It would now appear that Progressive Conservatives are following suit-oh, with great caution-but let us hope they will have the courage to support us in our efforts to bring the age of eligibility for the old age security pension down to 60.
I am raising this point because I was appalled to note, on March 28 last, barely two days ago, that all Progressive Conservatives voted with the Liberals against an amendment to bring the age of eligibility for the old age pension down to 60 while granting the same pension to the other spouse, of whatever age. The reason why we hoped for Progressive Conservative support on the occasion of the vote on March 28 is that the motion before us today has been on the order paper of the House for several weeks, but some political reversals have no other explanation than opportunism.
I recall that, on the occasion of that vote of March 28, Social Credit members were termed demagogues by the new Minister of National Health and Social Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and also by the spokesman for the official oppo-

sition. In fact, we worked to make the government bring forward a bill similar to the motion under study. I have always noticed that such words as "demagogues" and others like it are always the last arguments of a defenceless government.
Being more logical than two old parties and, consequently, not at all demagogues, we heartily congratulate the progressive conservative member and we urge him to be firm in order to convince once and for all his hon. colleagues of the merit of his motion and of our determination to fight to obtain the reform of the old age security plan.
The problem of the wife who is younger than her husband who has reached pensionable age is much more dramatic than some members suspect, particularly in Quebec. If this were an ordinary debate, I would have made a point of bringing letters I have received from my riding. I have hundreds of letters asking for the granting of a pension for a wife who is younger than her husband, because the Quebec Welfare Services are experiencing serious difficulties.
The situation may be better in other provinces. But, as I come from the province of Quebec and know what is happening there, I am specifically speaking about my province. In fact, the Quebec minister, Claude Caston-guay, is still convinced that a couple can live on $150 a month.
This is the reason why, when the federal government pays $150 or $156 a month, the wife who is younger cannot get anything from Quebec. The standard amount is a $150 a month. They are being told: whether you die or not, a payment of $150 is enough, so be comforted. Such is the democratic regime in Quebec, which is headed by former technocrats. We are all the more justified in protesting now that the pension has been increased to $170 a month, Mr. Speaker. If the wife is only 55, this means that the couple will have to live for five years on $170 a month. This couple will be lucky if it does not have to pay a special tax on the $20 increase.
I have already exposed in this House all the anti-social measures that the government takes pleasure in bringing before Parliament. The legislation on old age security pensions is a striking example.
When they do introduce a social reform, it is always in driblets, because all those measures are devised, worked out and prepared by technocrats who never came down among the people to learn its needs and because the government never listened closely to the expectations of the people, or if it did, it pretended not to hear anything.
In my opinion, both members of the government and the opposition hear from their constituencies. Surely, they must receive letters asking them for a reform. We can wait six years for a small reform. We have been yelling, asking, begging for six years, by proposing motions and amendments, and always we have been answered by fine words and nothing else. And the wives who are not yet 65 are still waiting for our social reforms, Mr. Speaker.
I said a while ago that all this was caused by a group of technocrats who don't really know the needs of the popu-
March 30, 1973

lation, while here they are all-powerful. If all our social reforms originated among the population, one can be sure that we could at last lay the foundations for a true social reform.
As long as the population will be governed by Ottawa mandarins who are very well paid all their life and unafraid of being attacked by the people, it will be impossible to pass the legislation which the population so badly needs.
The only solution is to give back to the member of Parliament full freedom of action and his responsibilities in his riding, that he might truly reflect the opinions and the will of his electors.
The ministers should remain strictly the servants of Parliament, instead of acting as screens, not to say flunkeys, of big financial interests.
Only on that condition will we pass in this House measures as humane as the one before us today.

Mr. Speaker, I will speak only briefly in this debate because it is obvious that all hon. members now in the House strongly support the intent of the motion. The hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Fox) referred to the recent statement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) in which he outlined the priorities of social welfare legislation. The first priority is to deal adequately and comprehensively with the special needs of the elderly, the physically handicapped and the blind who obviously are not in a position to take care of their own economic and financial needs. I couple this plea, Mr. Speaker, with the suggestion which has been made with respect to senior citizen, married couples. I trust the government will exercise the authority it possesses to bring before the House an adequate legislative program which will implement the criteria which the minister himself has described as of first importance, namely, legislation which will look after the needs of the elderly and the physically handicapped in a satisfactory way.
This is an area in which there need be no hesitancy on the part of the federal government. There is no jurisdictional dispute involved: it is exclusively the territory of the federal government. I trust that before this hour closes we shall have given unanimous consent to the resolution, thereby empowering the government to take necessary action.

Mr. Speaker, it would be difficult to oppose the spirit of the motion before us, because it recognizes a very real problem in our society. There are cases where a person of pensionable age has a spouse who is slightly below that age. Consequently, they have to live on one person's pension. This is
Old Age Security
a difficulty which has been considered by the government and is still under active consideration.
The motion before us goes beyond this point, however. It talks about a spouse married to someone of pensionable age being eligible to draw a pension regardless of his or her age. There may be situations in which the person of pensionable age is married to a spouse who is 20 years younger, to someone still a member of the work force. It seems to me that it would be more reasonable to suggest, for example, that spouses between 60 and 65 who are married to someone of pensionable age should be eligible for pension as though they were of pensionable age. It seems to me this would be more acceptable than taking a broad approach and saying that anyone in that category, regardless of age, should be entitled to a pension.
My feeling is that implementing such a program might easily give rise to difficulty and, perhaps, to some abuses. A spouse who received such a pension when she was young might, after the death of his or her partner, continue to be eligible for pension for a very long time. The department has given a good deal of thought to this matter, particularly in light of the forthcoming federal-provincial conference on social security at which it is intended to review the social security system in Canada.
When the original federal-provincial conference on this subject was held a month or so ago, the provinces asked the federal government not to make adjustments to the old age security and related programs by altering the age qualifications and making other adjustments. They felt there were other priorities which should be taken into account in ensuring that justice was done all the way around. They were afraid that if steps were taken of the kind suggested in the motion before us in the absence of consultation with the provinces, there might be no money available to meet other requirements and priorities which might be put forward.
As members know, there are other areas which must be considered in terms of priority; for instance, the family allowances scheme, the situation of the working poor, the needs of the handicapped, touched upon by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), to mention only three. All these needs must be considered in relationship to each other, and it seems to me it would be improper at this time for the government to take a position with respect to one problem, even though it is an important human problem, and say it proposes to deal with it in a particular way, before the provinces have had an opportunity to review the whole question with us and reach a common decision which will take all priorities into consideration. It seems to me that in terms of national unity alone, the federal government ought to give consideration to the views of the provinces when fixing priorities.
As I say, the government is concerned about this problem and is giving it immediate consideration. We shall be attending the conference to be held during Easter week, which is not far away, when all these matters will be brought forward, and we shall be proposing an over-all approach to social security which, hopefully, will establish the right kind of priorities so that not only senior citizens but the working poor and those who are unable to work at all, such as the handicapped, are dealt with fairly. We would then be able to proceed with a plan which

It is our conviction that the points we have in common in our respective political philosophies, our particular location in the world, and the complementary aspects of our economies will allow us to establish increasingly deeper bonds.
For you, as for us, democracy is a way of life. It implies absolute respect for different forms of thought. It also means respect for self-determination of peoples, coexistence and even cooperation between states with different ideologies.
Freedom is not an abstract capacity to take decisions, but a concrete possibility of implementing these decisions. In the same way in which an unjust society actually annuls all freedoms, unfair relations among peoples condemn the poorest to a virtual loss of autonomy.
The true democratic ideal calls for each man and each nation to have the means to satisfy their needs and develop their personality; to exercise effectively the rights they have as individuals, human groups and nations.

We are certain that a new international society is in the process of being built. Small and medium-sized countries must participate in this era of transition by renewing and1 strengthening their nationalistic attitude; they must also acquire new instruments to make their full development feasible.
If we have overcome the colonial mentality domestically, we should do the same in our relations with other countries. We must weigh with serenity the changes that are taking place on the world scene and act with flexibility and courage in favor of our national objectives.
The end of the cold war and of bipolarism points to a different political structure characterized by the emergence of new centers of power, by the establishment of more flexible alliances and by a greater participation on the part of developing countries in the management of world affairs.
Only dangerous fatalism could' lead us to believe that the international community should be structured in the future in accordance with old systems of domination and that the only possible way of change would be to redefine spheres of influence. Such a belief would mean facing the future with a nineteenth century outlook and condemning ourselves irrevocably to dependence.
On the contrary, we believe that countries like ours are called upon to play a more significant role in the field of international relations, not only because of their rate of development, their unexploited wealth or demographic growth, but also because of the enormous possibilities of concerted action and the moral force of a behaviour which adheres to the standards of public international law.
Neither of our countries wants to arouse systematic opposition or enmity with any nation. We hope, from similar positions, to modify hemisphere relations in order to share prosperity in a better way. We realize that this option means not only basic modifications in our relations with other countries of the continent, but also a definite extension of our contacts to other areas of the world.

Moreover, we share many of the doubts that rightly concern Canada with respect to this organization. We realize that its decisions only appeared to be democratic and that ideological intolerance frequently diverted this institution from its objectives. Neo-colonial attitudes and international injustice will not decrease substantially over a short period. It will take time to overcome inertia and certain barriers. The best way to do this is by extending exchanges and unifying the positions among countries that have interests which are alike.
For years, Canada and Mexico have had similar attitudes on some of the most important questions of our time. Both our countries are concerned, for instance, about finding formulas to harmonize industrial growth with the conservation of the human environment and natural resources.
Air, water and land pollution becomes a new source of servitude when it is the result of relations with more industrialized countries. Ecological aggressions which cause serious damage to life, health and the economy are an additional load for less developed nations to bear.
Economic sovereignty is one of the expressions of political sovereignty. That is why we affirm the unalienable right of all countries to defend and exploit their basic resources. Therefore we fight for the establishment of a regime of international protection of the environment through regional and international agreements that take into account the legitimate right of States.
The desire on the part of many countries to extend the limits of the territorial sea is a growing and legitimate one. Mexico grants priority to the need to establish a zone of exclusive exploitation for coastal states.
We believe that a new maritime system to establish the rights of coastal states with fairness and precision is indispensable, in view of the present-day needs, and the nature of the conflicts that arise from the possibility that some countries have to exploit their own wealth and that of others.
I would like to give special emphasis, in the presence of this assembly, to the pleasure of my government at the growing affinity of our two countries on these subjects, and on the interest Mexico takes in the valuable precedent Canada has set by establishing a system for the protection and preservation of the maritime species that inhabit the arctic region.
The general and universally compulsory standards that would govern both rights to the sea and the protection of the environment should be included in the Charter of the Economic Rights and Duties of States which is now being drafted by a group of forty countries at the request of the United Nations.
When, at the Third United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, we proposed the adoption of this document by the international community, Mexico outlined the principles of international equity that come from the struggle of the people of the Third World and which are a basic requirement for harmonious coexistence among States.
In an interdependent world, the strategic problem for developing countries is to reorient the trend of their growing trade. We insist that it is necessary for the genrespetuoso de la soberania de sus Estados miembros y porque, entre sus tareas, ocupe un lugar preponderante la cooperation economica y social.

Canada y Mexico han tenido, durante anos actitudes similares en algunas de las cuestiones mas importantes de esta epoca. A nuestros dos paises preocupa, por ejemplo, encontrar las formulas que permitan armonizar el creci-miento industrial y la preservation del medio humano y de los recursos naturales.

A las pesadas cargas que soportan los pueblos de menor desarrollo, se suma ahora la agresion ecologica que lesiona gravemente su vida, su salud y su economia.
La soberania economica es una de las expresiones de la soberania politica. Por eso afirmamos el derecho inalienable de todos los pueblos a la defensa y a la explotacion de sus recursos b&sicos. Pugnamos, en consecuencia, por el establecimiento de un regimen de proteccion internacional al medio ambiente, conformado por acuerdos regionales y mundiales que toman en cuenta el legitimo derecho de los Estados.
Es creciente y legitima la pretension de muchos paises por extender los limites del mar territorial. Mexico otorga una atencion prioritaria a la necesidad de establecer una zona de explotacion exclusiva para el Estado ribereno.
Estimamos indispensable la estructuracion de un nuevo regimen maritimo que fije con equidad y precision los derechos de los Estados riberenos, considerando las necesidades contemporaneas y la naturaleza de los con-flictos que suscita la potencialidad de algunas naciones para explotar sus propias riquezas y las ajenas.
Deseo subrayar, ante esta asamblea el beneplacito con que ve mi gobierno la creciente afinidad de nuestros dos paises sobre estos temas. Asimismo, el interes con que Mexico contempla el valioso precedente sentado por Canada al determinar un sistema de proteccion y preservacion de las especies maritimas que habitan la region artica.
Las normas generales y universalmente obligatorias que regirian, tanto el derecho del mar como el de la proteccion del medio ambiente, deberan contenerse en la Carta de los Deberes y Derechos Economicos de los Estados que ahora se formula por un grupo de cuarenta paises por encomienda de las Naciones Unidas.
Al proponer en la III Conferencia sobre Comercio y Desarrollo la adoption de este documento por la comuni-dad internacional, Mexico delineo aquellos principios de equidad derivados de la lucha emprendida por los pueblos del Tercer Mundo y que constituyen requisitos basicos para una convivencia armonica entre los Estados.
En un mundo interdependiente, el problema estrategico para los paises en vias de desarrollo consiste en reorientar el sentido de sus crecientes intercambios economicos.

Advantages in trade proportional to the varying degrees of development, are not only a valuable stimulus for the participation of our countries in the large markets, but also a means to accelerate industrialization throughout vast regions of the world and to promote domestic changes in countries that have lagged behind. The control of the State over the main economic processes is a necessary condition to maintain the autonomy of its political decisions. That is why there is a general concern to study and regulate the characteristics of foreign investment and of ways to absorb technological resources.
Given the stage of evolution of Canada and Mexico, this subject is of decisive importance. Almost simultaneously, both countries have begun systematic research on the effects of an excessive concentration of foreign capital and technology and have adopted or are about to adopt measures to reorganize the participation of these factors in their economic life.
My country's Congress has recently approved a law that promotes national investment and regulates foreign investment. This legislation reflects the different stages of our nationalistic effort. It retains old provisions under which we do not allow foreign investment in strategic spheres of the national economy. Moreover, it defines the economic activities in which foreign capital must be in the minority. It establishes the technical instruments and powers that permit the restriction, orientation or, if necessary, encouragement of capital flow to adjust it to our own objectives of development. Finally, it prevents the acquisition of Mexican enterprises that are functioning efficiently.
Another law for the registration of the transference of technology and the use and exploitation of patents and trade-marks complements our policy on this subject. Within a framework of independence we shall accept and use technology insofar as it adjusts to the aims of our economic policy. We shall try to eliminate practices or stipulations that limit our exports, prevent the development of our own technology, make production more expensive or hinder our autonomous development. In short, we want technology to be an instrument of progress, not of subjection.

Decision-making centers must remain within the nation, since to proceed otherwise would be to deny our independence and' to deviate from the objectives of development. Mexico will give full support to any initiative that is taken to draw up an obligatory Code of conduct that will regulate the actions of the multinational corporations and establish guidelines for the domestic legislation of the nations concerned. In our era a vigorous economic nationalism with characteristics that are different from those of previous stages has been reborn. Then, it was a matter of conquering the effective use of the fundamental rights of soveignty; of recovering ownership of land and of basic resources; of carrying out essential structural reforms that would cancel out our feudal past and open the way to the advent of an industrial society.
The changes I refer to came from popular movements, which were sometimes violent, or from the establishment of domestic policies that caused deep divisions. On implementing these, countries like ours became isolated from the community of nations and had to struggle alone.
Nationalism today, differently from yesterday, is also an internationalism. It means strengthening the bonds among peoples that have similar needs and aspirations. It represents an effort to make the interests of different and heterogeneous countries coincide and to defend them in solidarity on a world scale.
However, we know that a nationalistic stand held only abroad has no real basis. True nationalism, the nationalism that Mexico and Canada practice, is an effort to achieve social integration and coordination. This nationalism can be measured by the internal cohesion of a community, and by the degree of understanding which prevails among its people, the equality of their living conditions and their effective participation in their common tasks.
